name: example-two-lans
description:
Two LANs joined by a router: **r-gw** routes between LAN 1 (**sw1**, `10.0.1.0/24`) and LAN 2 (**sw2**, `10.0.2.0/24`), and gives both internet access through NAT.

| Container | Address | Role |
|---|---|---|
| r-gw | `10.0.1.1`, `10.0.2.1` | router and NAT to the internet |
| lin-pc | `10.0.1.10` | Linux PC with a desktop |
| serv-www | `10.0.2.10` | web server |

## Open lin-pc's desktop
After **Deploy**, open `https://<Docker host>:3001` in your PC's browser (click r-gw: the *Port mappings* section has the link) and accept the self-signed certificate warning.

> [!NOTE]
> The first Deploy downloads the desktop image (about 1.5 GB), so it takes a while.

> [!TIP]
> The desktop is encoded as video on the Docker host's CPU: give the VM 4 vCPUs if it feels slow. Its frame rate is capped at 30 by `SELKIES_FRAMERATE` in lin-pc's Environment.

## Try it
1. On lin-pc's desktop, open Firefox and browse to `http://10.0.2.10`. The page comes from serv-www, through r-gw.
2. In a terminal on lin-pc, trace the path (it goes through `10.0.1.1`), then reach the internet through r-gw's NAT:
   ```
   traceroute -n 10.0.2.10
   curl -I https://example.com
   ```
3. Capture the **r-gw–sw2** cable while reloading the page: the source is `10.0.1.10`, because r-gw routes between the LANs without NAT.
4. Capture the **r-gw–sw1** cable: the desktop's own traffic (TCP 3001) is there too, because the desktop is reached through r-gw. Filter it out in Wireshark with:
   ```
   not tcp.port == 3001
   ```

## Questions
- [ ] Why does traffic between the LANs keep its source address, but traffic to the internet doesn't?
- [ ] On serv-www, remove the default route (`ip route del default`). Which tests break, and why?

nodes.name: r-gw
nodes.startup:
# Outbound: masquerade both LANs behind r-gw's nat0 address
nat-on

# Inbound: the Docker host's port 3001 is published to r-gw's port 3001 on nat0;
# forward it to lin-pc's desktop, so the desktop is reached through the gateway like any other service
iptables -t nat -C PREROUTING -i nat0 -p tcp --dport 3001 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.0.1.10:3001 2>/dev/null \
  || iptables -t nat -A PREROUTING -i nat0 -p tcp --dport 3001 -j DNAT --to-destination 10.0.1.10:3001

nodes.name: lin-pc
nodes.startup:
# r-gw is the way out of LAN 1
ip route replace default via 10.0.1.1
echo nameserver 1.1.1.1 > /etc/resolv.conf

nodes.name: serv-www
nodes.startup:
# r-gw is the way out of LAN 2 ip route replace default via 10.0.2.1 echo nameserver 1.1.1.1 > /etc/resolv.conf # The web page, then the web server (BusyBox httpd on port 80, serving /var/www) cat > /var/www/index.html < serv-www

Hello from $(hostname)

Served by BusyBox httpd at 10.0.2.10 on LAN 2, reached through r-gw.

HTML pkill -x httpd 2>/dev/null; busybox-extras httpd -p 80 -h /var/www

notes.text:
lin-pc's desktop: https://<Docker host>:3001
Docker host :3001 → r-gw (nat0)
→ DNAT → lin-pc 10.0.1.10:3001

images.dockerlab/router:latest:
FROM alpine:latest

# Networking tools for a gateway or router
RUN apk add --no-cache iproute2 iptables tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils

# nat-on: masquerade traffic leaving through the NAT interface (nat0).
# Safe to run more than once; use it in startup commands.
RUN printf '%s\n' '#!/bin/sh' \
      'iptables -t nat -C POSTROUTING -o nat0 -j MASQUERADE 2>/dev/null || iptables -t nat -A POSTROUTING -o nat0 -j MASQUERADE' \
      > /usr/local/bin/nat-on && chmod +x /usr/local/bin/nat-on
images.dockerlab/web:latest:
FROM alpine:latest

# A small web server (BusyBox httpd), plus the end-host tools: full ip, packet capture, DNS lookups, web requests
RUN apk add --no-cache busybox-extras iproute2 tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils
RUN mkdir -p /var/www
images.dockerlab/desktop:latest:
FROM lscr.io/linuxserver/webtop:latest

# An XFCE desktop in the browser (Selkies, HTTPS on port 3001), plus a web browser
# and the end-host network tools: full ip, packet capture, DNS lookups, web requests, ping
RUN apk add --no-cache firefox iproute2 tcpdump bind-tools curl iputils
